notes.text: This line is built for players who like answering d4 with d5.
notes.original: This line will be tailored for players that prefer 1...d5 as their main opening against d4.

notes.text: White develops the bishop first, so e3 can later support d4 without trapping it.
notes.original:
White develops the dark-square bishop. Developing the bishop first allows White to support their d4-pawn with e3, without trapping this bishop behind the pawn chain.

This is the beginning of the London system. The appeal of this system is that White can go for the same general set-up in response to most of Black's replies (see diagram). General plans for White include planting their kingside knight on e5, controlled by d4 and the dark-square bishop. Often White's light-square bishop is sacrificed on h7 to open up a castled king, followed by Qh5+.

Formally, the Accelerated London follows 1...d5, but the London set up can be played against 1...Nf6 just as well and may transpose if Black plays d5.

At higher levels, the move order 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bf4 to reach the London system is more common.

The main alternative for White is the Rapport-Jobava London system, with Nc3 (in either order, 2.Nc3 & 3.Bf4 or 2.Bf4 & 3.Nc3) where plans include the knight coordinating with the f4 bishop to attack c7, and an early e4.

Because White can play the same system in response to most of Black's replies, White usually continues 3.e3, 4.c3, 5.Nd2 etc regardless. Most move orders are interchangeable.

The idea behind the 3...e6 line is to play 4...Bd6, getting ready to castle quickly and threatening to trade off White's London bishop. White can drop their bishop back to g3, inviting Black to trade but after hxg3 White gets the semi-open h-file in return. In the e6 lines, Black's light square bishop often has difficulty developing. This approach resembles a Semi-Slav defence with colours reversed.

Having committed to d5 already, the King's Indian-style approach with 3...g6 is less common but still playable. Black continues 4...Bg7, and 5...O-O. White usually includes h3, so there is a retreat square for their bishop on h2, and Be2.

Possibly the earliest example of 1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 was given by Jacob Sarratt in his 1808 book A Treatise on the Game of Chess. This continued 2...Bf5 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.f3.

James Mason pioneered the London system continuation (i.e. where White plays e3, places a knight on d2 and their light square bishop on d3 or e2) in the 1882 Vienna tournament. It became known as the London after the 1922 London tournament, where it was played by Capablanca and others.

The London system is popular with amateurs. It is often recommended to beginners as White can develop in the same way irrespective of how Black chooses to respond. It is occasionally seen at the highest levels of chess, e.g. in Ding v Nepomniachtchi in their 2023 World Championship match.

A recent innovation is to combine Bf4 and Nc3, the Rapport-Jobava London, developed by Richárd Rapport and Baduur Jobava.

notes.text: White's knight move will likely transpose into familiar lines once you reply with your knight.
notes.original: This will likely transpose after....

notes.text: This is your most common reply; next you choose between c5 and e6.
notes.original: Black's most common reply is 2...Nf6, then they have two main approaches: 3...c5 or 3...e6.

notes.text: Your c-pawn offers a gambit; you aim for counterplay against b2 with the bishop and queen.
notes.original:
The ...c5 line (either 3...c5, or in the order 2...c5 3.e6 Nf6) is called the Steinitz countergambit. Black's idea is to prioritise ...Bf5 and ...Qb6 before they finish developing the kingside and castling. Black seeks counterplay by pressuring b2, which White left undefended when they moved their bishop early on. (White does not want to take the offered c5 pawn of course: they'd rather play c3 and let Black trade into them, so that they can keep two pawns in the centre).

Black challenges the centre with c5, the Steinitz countergambit, offering White their c-pawn.

As the pawn is already defended by the Queen, White does not actually need to defend it further: if 3.Nc3 cxd4 4.Qxd4 and White is threatening to win Black's d-pawn: 4...Nc6? 5.Qxd5 Qxd5 6.Nxd5 (if 4...e6 5.Bxb8! Rxb8 and White's centralised queen is unassailable).

Other London system-moves 3.c3 or 3.Nf3 may be played and usually transpose.

Accepting the gambit, 3.dxc5?!, is unwise. By taking the pawn, White reduces their control over the centre and Black can easily recover the pawn. Mason, pioneer of the London system, fell into this in his game against Steinitz in 1883. It continued like this: 3.dxc5?! Nc6 4.Nf3 f6 5.e3 e5 6.Bg3 Bxc5 (see diagram).

A rare sideline here is the Morris countergambit, 3.e4. White gives up their e-pawn in order to push d5 and cramp Black's position. This resembles an Albin Countergambit with colours reversed.

notes.text: This is the London System: White plays the same setup whatever you choose, so you need a good answer.
notes.original:
: The initial position of the London System.
The London System is an incredibly popular low-level opening, often chosen by newer players just learning opening theory and still mastering the basics of piece movement. By playing this system, white can usually play the same set of moves regardless of how black chooses to respond. This ubiquity only sacrifices a little bit of white's initial tempo advantage, and practically white usually will know relatively more opening theory since the position is easier for white than black. However, at high-level, this opening gives up too much of white's initial advantage, often leading to draws. Therefore, it is usually avoided at high-level. Black has several options in which to respond to the London System:

notes.text: Build solidly with e6, Be7 and castling, and challenge White's bishop later with c5 or Nh5.
notes.original:
The London System is a solid and flexible opening system for white that can be played against various setups by black. After the moves:

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Nf6 3.e3 or

The main ideas for both sides in the London System's main line are:

Development and Structure: Nf3, Be2, c3, and often Nbd2 followed by a potential e4 break or the more restrained h3 and O-O. The pawn on d4 and the pawn on e3 provide a solid central structure.

Queenside Expansion: With moves like a4-a5 or a queenside pawn storm with b4, aiming for a potential minority attack.

King Safety: Usually achieved with O-O. The rook on f1 might later swing over to the c-file or e-file.

Central Break: Depending on Black's setup, White can aim for e4 at some point.

Challenge the Bishop: ...c5 or ...Nh5 can be played to challenge White's strong Bf4.

Development: e6 followed by Be7, O-O, and Nbd7 or Nc6. Depending on the situation, the light-squared bishop can be developed to d7, f5, or g4.

Central Control: Black usually maintains a pawn on d5 and can consider playing ...e5 under the right conditions.

Queenside Counterplay: Black can look for counterplay with moves like ...a6 and ...b5, depending on White's play. For a general introduction to the London System, take a closer look at 1.d4 d5 2.Bf4

notes.text: Your c-pawn hits d4 right away; White gains little by grabbing it, since you can win it back.
notes.original: Main Line. Black's most common, strong response. This immediately contests the center by putting pressure on d4, temporarily gambiting the c-pawn. White doesn't yet want to open the center as it isn't finished developing, so capturing the gambited c5 pawn isn't beneficial for white, as it can be easily recaptured with a later Bxc5. While theoretically as strong as several other responses, this response sees slightly better practical results comparatively, even at high-level.

notes.text: Your e6 pawn solidly guards d5, but it shuts in your light-squared bishop.
notes.original: French Variation. Black's 2nd most common, strong response. This solidly defends the d5 pawn similarly to the French Defense, forming a central pawn chain. This comes at a slight cost: the "French" light-squared bishop is now somewhat obstructed and will have difficulty being brought into the game.

notes.text: Your bishop gets out before you close the chain with e6, at a small cost in time.
notes.original: Black's 3rd most common, strong response. This develops the light-squared bishop outside of black's central pawn structure before closing the chain with e6. This enables black to activate its weak "French" bishop, though this comes at a slight tempo loss.

notes.text: This guards d5 but wastes a tempo, since you would rather hit d4 with c5.
notes.original: Slav Variation. Inaccuracy. This defends the d5 pawn, similarly to the Slav Defense. However, white now has a lead in development and space which it can now more easily consolidate. Additionally, black will often want to begin to attack white's pawn center with c5, which means this wastes a tempo defending the d5 pawn.

notes.text: You prepare to fianchetto your bishop on g7, a Grünfeld-style setup pressuring d4.
notes.original: Grunfeld Variation. Uncommon, strong response. This prepares to fianchetto black's dark-squared bishop, resulting in black's position resembling the Grunfeld Defense. The fianchettoed "Grunfeld" bishop will exert strong pressure along the main a1-h8 diagonal, putting pressure on the d4 pawn and x-raying white's a1 rook.

notes.text: Your bishop hits the knight, but it isn't pinned, so Ne5 answers from a strong square.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Mistake. This attempts to aggressively develop the light-squared bishop outside of black's central pawn structure before closing it with e6, while also pressuring white's f3 knight, possibly pinning it to the queen if the e2 pawn moves. However, the knight isn't pinned, and can counterattack the bishop with Ne5, centralizing the knight and reaching a semi-outpost that can't easily be attacked with a pawn.

notes.text: White supports d4 and frees the light bishop so it can develop and castle.
notes.original: White's strongest, most common response. This supports the d4 pawn, opening up the light-squared bishop so that it can develop and white can later castle king's side.

notes.text: White's c3 guards d4 but develops nothing, giving you time to add pressure with Nc6.
notes.original: White's 2nd most common response. Inaccuracy. This supports the d4 pawn and obstructs any checks on the white king. However, this doesn't develop a piece, prevents white from ever castling queen's side, and doesn't bring white closer to castling king's side. This gives black extra tempo to put pressure on d4 with Nc6.

notes.text: White's pawn grab is a mistake: play e6 to defend d5, then win the c5 pawn back with your bishop.
notes.original: White's 3rd most common response. Mistake. This captures black's gambited c-pawn. However, black can easily recapture the pawn with Bxc5 after closing its pawn chain and defending d5 with e6, similarly to the French Defense. White also now has a more difficult time controlling the center, having essentially given up a central pawn for a side pawn. Additionally, white loses positional advantage if it tries to hang onto the pawn c5.

notes.text: Your pawn guards d5 and opens the bishop's path to win back the c5 pawn.
Your knight adds pressure on d4 and covers b4, so you can regain the c5 pawn later.
notes.original: Black's most common, strong response. This develops the queen's side knight, putting more pressure on white's d4 pawn while obstructing any checks on the king by white's light-squared bishop. This gambits the c5 pawn, but the knight defends against b4 which is the only way to easily maintain defense of the pawn before black later recaptures with Bxc5.

notes.text: Your queen hits b2 and guards c5, but White can attack the unsupported d5 pawn with c4.
notes.original: Black's 2nd most common response. This aggressively develops the queen, putting more pressure on the d4 pawn, attacking the b2 pawn, and defending the c5 pawn. However, since black hasn't supported the d5 pawn, white can attack it with c4. Black can trade pawns with cxd4, but white can tactically offer a queen trade with Qxd4, leaving white with a massive developmental advantage if black trades queens.

notes.text: Trading on d4 opens the center; you argue the extra space is as good as a closed position.
notes.original: Black's 3rd most common, strong response. This immediately reduces tension in the center by trading pawns, opening up the center somewhat. Black argues that the additional space is just as advantageous as the more closed position.

notes.text: Your bishop and queen now guard c5 and the knight, though your light bishop is hemmed in.
notes.original: French Defense transposition. Black's 4th most common response, though it is the most common when considering transpositions. This solidly defends the e5 pawn and opens up the diagonals for both the dark-squared bishop and the queen, which defend the c5 pawn and knight, respectively. It comes at the cost of somewhat obstructing the light-squared bishop, whose weakness is usually referred to as the "French" bishop.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the knight to the queen, but dxc5 wins a pawn and leaves White ahead.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Inaccuracy. This pins the f3 knight to white's queen, preventing the knight from moving. However, white can simply trade pawns with dxc5, reducing the need to move the f3 knight to defend the d4 square. It also wins a pawn that can be defended with b4 in exchange for some slight positional weakness, leaving white still ahead. White could also counterattack black's king with Bb5+.

notes.text: This leaves your c5 pawn hanging: White takes it, defends with b4, and is a pawn up.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Slight blunder. This hangs the c5 pawn to dxc5, which can't be recaptured before white defends it with b4, leaving white a pawn up.

notes.text: This stops Bb5 ideas but leaves your c5 pawn hanging, and White can keep it with b4.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Mistake. This defends the b5 square, preventing any Bb5 checks or pins on the knight after Nc6 or Nbd7. However, this hangs the c5 pawn, which white can capture and defend with b4 for the cost of some positional advantage.

notes.text: White's usual reply: a solid pawn triangle guards d4, and the knight will go to d2 instead.
notes.original: White's most common response. This solidly but passively defends the d4 pawn, forming a pawn triangle which is a staple position of the London System. This comes at a slight cost of obstructing the usual development of white's queen's side knight, but white often wants to develop with Nbd2 anyway.

notes.text: White's knight guards f3 and c4 while leaving the c-pawn free to move.
notes.original: White's 2nd most common, strong response, seen more at high-level. Similar to the Tarrasch Variation of the French Defense, this develops the knight unusually but in a way that accomplishes much. It defends the other f3 knight, it doesn't obstruct the c-pawn (like Nc3) which enables c3 or c4, it defends c4 to help enable playing c4, it moves the knight to allow white's rook to move if necessary, and it can easily move to b3 if black decides to trade pawns in the center with cxd4, putting a lot of pressure on d4. This comes at a cost of temporarily obstructing the queen's defense of d4.

notes.text: White's knight hits d5 but blocks its own c-pawn, so you can play Bg4 before e6.
notes.original: White's 3rd most common response. Inaccuracy. This develops the queen's side knight, putting pressure on the d5 pawn. However, this obstructs the c-pawn, preventing white from as effectively attack black's center and giving black some tempo to move its light-squared bishop outside of the pawn center with Bg4 before closing it with e6, transposing to a superior French Defense structure.

notes.text: White's bishop pins your knight, but Qa5+ hits back at the bishop with check.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Inaccuracy. This develops the light-squared bishop, pinning black's knight to its king. However, black can tactically counterattack the bishop with Qa5+, forcing Nc6 to obstruct the check and defend the bishop. This knight then can be attacked with Ne4, forcing the bishop to trade with the knight and doubling white's pawns after Nxc3.

notes.text: A simple, strong developing move: White gets closer to castling before the center opens.
notes.original: Uncommon, strong response. This simply develops the light-squared bishop, bringing white closer to castling king's side before the center opens up.

notes.text: A mistake: play Bg4 to pin the knight, and White can't hold c4 and break the pin.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Mistake. This attacks black's d4 pawn, offering a pawn trade to open up the center. However, black can tactically overload white's light-squared bishop by pinning white's f3 knight with Bg4. White can't obstruct the pin (allowing white's knight to move) without allowing black to capture the c4 pawn with dxc4, forcing the light-squared bishop to recapture. This tactic allows black to open up the center advantageously without white's knight being able to support it.

notes.text: White takes the c5 pawn and can't easily keep it, since your knight covers b4.
notes.original: Uncommon response, seen more at high-level. This simply reduces tension in the center by capturing black's gambited pawn. White can't easily defend this pawn as b4 is covered by the c6 knight, but this doesn't lose any tempo as black must also recapture it, and white argues that the more open center is easier to win tactically.

notes.text: Your queen hits the b2 pawn and guards your c5 pawn: a strong, common choice.
notes.original: Black's most common, strong response. This aggressively develops the queen to an active square, putting more pressure on the d4 pawn, attacking the b2 pawn, and defending the c5 pawn.

notes.text: Your knight hits the bishop on f4 and threatens to trade it, costing White the bishop pair.
notes.original: Black's uncommon, strong response. This attacks the light-squared bishop, threatening to trade it for a knight. The bishop usually (eventually) retreats to g3 to open up white's rook when black finally captures the bishop, at the cost of the bishop pair.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the f3 knight to the queen, threatening to take it and give up the bishop pair.
notes.original: Black's 2nd most common response, seen more at low-level due to fewer draws (which are relatively advantageous for black) and slightly more difficult play. This develops the light-squared bishop, pinning white's f3 knight to its queen. Black threatens to gambit its bishop pair by trading with Bxf3, displacing the queen to the king's side to recapture and allowing black to begin a queen's side attack with Qb6.

notes.text: A solid but slightly inaccurate move: it opens lines for your bishop and queen but boxes in your light bishop.
notes.original: Black's 3rd most common response, and most common response when considering transpositions. Inaccuracy. This solidly defends the e5 pawn and opens up the diagonals for both the dark-squared bishop and the queen, which defend the c5 pawn and knight, respectively. However, it comes at the cost of somewhat obstructing the light-squared bishop, whose weakness is usually referred to as the "French" bishop. Additionally, it gives white time to deal with its dark-squared bishop, which it currently can't prevent being traded for a knight, losing white the bishop pair.

notes.text: A slight blunder: your bishop is out, but the c5 pawn hangs to dxc5, and b4 is backed by c3.
notes.original: Black's 4th most common response, seen more at low-level. Slight blunder. This develops the light-squared bishop outside of black's pawn center, which it will close with e6. However, this leaves the c5 pawn hanging, allowing white to capture it with dxc5 since white can now play b4 since it is defended by the c3 pawn.

notes.text: Trading on d4 opens the center slightly, but gains you nothing while White is close to castling.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Inaccuracy. This reduces tension in the center, trading the gambited c5 pawn and opening the center slightly. However, since white is closer to castling king's side, black only wants to open the center if it can gain additional advantage, which this doesn't.

notes.text: The fianchetto prep wastes two tempi, since your bishop would only stare at three pawns.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Inaccuracy. This prepares to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop. However, doing so doesn't really give much advantage to black as the bishop will be staring at three pawns along the major a1-h8 diagonal. Because of this, this is essentially a waste of two tempo, which white can use to solidify its position and prepare to attack black's relatively weaker center.

notes.text: A mistake: a6 stops Bb5, but White can take c5 with dxc5 and support it with b4.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Mistake. This defends the b5 square, preventing any Bb5 checks or pins on the knight after Nc6 or Nbd7. However, this hangs the c5 pawn, which white can capture (at the cost of some positional advantage) and defend with b4 since it is defended by the c3 pawn.

notes.text: White's queen offers a trade and eyes d5, but you can decline with c4, hitting the queen.
notes.original: White's most common response. Inaccuracy. This aggressively develops the queen, obstructing the black queen's attack on the b2 pawn by offering a queen trade. Black can't trade queens without opening up white's a1 rook after axb3. This also puts pressure on the d5 pawn if black declines the trade. However, black can decline the trade, as white also can't capture black's queen without opening up black's a8 rook after axb6. Because of this, black can force white to move its queen by attacking it with c4, essentially giving black a pawn tempo and cramping white's position in exchange for keeping the center intact by preventing cxd4.

notes.text: The queen guards b2 and takes an active post, making queenside play harder for you.
notes.original: White's 2nd most common, strong response. This defends the b2 pawn while also developing the queen to an active square, able to control the b1-h7 and a4-d1 diagonals. This prevents black from attacking on the queen's side as easily due to both fewer available squares and the threat of a later king's side attack by white. This also creates long term pressure along the c-file and brings white closer to connecting its rooks.

notes.text: Pushing b3 costs White something: you can break open the center with cxd4, a French-like structure better for you.
notes.original: White's 3rd most common response, seen more at low-level due to high draws at high-level. This defends the b-pawn by advancing it to the b3 square, now defended by both white's queen and a2 pawn. This comes at a slight cost of allowing black to break open the center with cxd4, essentially transposing to a worse-for-white variation of the French Defense with best play.

notes.text: A solid, more passive queen move that guards b2 and avoids easy trades against it.
notes.original: White's 4th most common, strong response. This also defends the b2 pawn while developing the queen to an active square. While more passive than Qc2, this is more solid, preventing black from easily attacking any of white's pieces without equivalent trades.

notes.text: White offers the b2 pawn for queenside play, but c4 is a simpler positional answer.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Inaccuracy. This develops the queen's side knight, gambiting the b2 pawn in return for an attack on black's queen side. If black captures with Qxb2, long term, best play trades a knight, rook and pawn for black's queen. Additionally, white has more developed pieces but black has a passed pawn. However, black can instead simply gain a stronger positional advantage with c4 instead, even if this is slightly weaker than Qxb2.

notes.text: A slight blunder: take on b2, and after Nbd2 you can also win the c3 pawn.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Slight blunder. This breaks tension in the center by attempting to trade pawns. However, this allows black to instead capture the b2 pawn with Qxb2, forcing white to play Nbd2 to defend the a1 rook. This then allows black to capture the c3 pawn.

notes.text: A mistake: Ne4 centralizes your knight with tempo by attacking the queen.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Mistake. This develops the queen, defending the b2 pawn and bringing white closer to connecting the rooks. However, this allows black to centralize the knight with tempo by attacking the queen with Ne4. Alternatively, black can continue to break open the center and use the queen as a target for a small positional advantage.

notes.text: A mistake: both the b2 and c3 pawns hang, though White wins back some compensation.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Mistake. This develops the queen's side knight, defending the f3 knight, defending the center, and preparing to move the knight to b3. However, this hangs both the b2 and c3 pawns after Qxb2 and then Qxb3. This loses two pawns, but gains a small positional advantage in return, often winning one of the pawns back, but still ending net negative.

notes.text: Your pawn hits White's queen, so it has to trade or step back.
Bg5 is a mistake: after the trade you freeze White's doubled pawns with g4, and Black usually wins in practice.
notes.original: White's most common response at all levels. Mistake. White moves its dark-squared bishop to g5, forcing black to chase it to g3 with its pawns in order to trade the bishop for the knight. This seems like an advantage over Bg3 initially, but black can freeze white's doubled pawn structure by playing g4 after the trade, and later h5 when the f3 knight moves. This combined with the fact the pawns are so advanced usually is enough for black to win practically.

notes.text: White retreats so that after your Nxg3 trade, hxg3 opens the h-file against your kingside.
notes.original: White's 2nd most common, strong response. This retreats the bishop so that when black trades with Nxg3, white can open up its rook file with hxg3, putting pressure on black's king's side which is where black will usually castle.

notes.text: White's bishop wants a trade with your c6 knight, keeping its pawns and leaving your other knight on the edge.
notes.original: White's 3rd most common, strong response. This tries to exchange the bishop with the c6 knight instead of the h5 knight, allowing white to preserve its pawn structure and leave black's remaining knight on the edge of the board. Black can avoid this by pushing away the bishop (back to g3) with f6, but white argues that this damages black's king's side pawn structure, so is worth playing.

notes.text: White grabs the c5 pawn; after your Nxf4 it loses the bishop pair and its pawns suffer, so it's equal.
notes.original: Uncommon, strong response, seen more at high-level. This neglects to move the light-squared bishop in favor of capturing the gambited c5 pawn. Black can't easily recapture the pawn with Bxc5 as white can defend it with b4. In return, white gives up its bishop pair following Nxf4 and accepts fairly significant damage to its pawn structure, leading to an equal position.

notes.text: You trade your knight for White's London bishop and keep both of your own.
Your h-pawn hits the bishop and forces it to h4, avoiding a bad trade on f4.
notes.original: Black's most common response. This simply forces white's bishop to h4 to avoid being traded disadvantageously on f4.

notes.text: White has to retreat to h4 to avoid a poor trade or losing the bishop.
notes.original: White's most common response. Again, white must retreat to h4 in order to avoid a positionally poor trade or lose the bishop.

notes.text: Your g-pawn pressures the bishop, forcing it to retreat to g3 or sacrifice itself.
notes.original: Black's most common response. This further pressures the dark-squared bishop, forcing it to retreat to g3 or sacrifice itself.

notes.text: This retreat is an inaccuracy: you can trade with Nxg3, and White could give up the bishop better.
notes.original: White's most common response. Inaccuracy. This simply retreats the bishop, allowing the Nxg3 trade in order to open up the h-file for white's rook. However, white can more advantageously give up the bishop since white's queen x-rays black's h5 knight.

notes.text: A blunder: the queen now hits your h5 knight, but Qb6 hits b2 and traps White's a1 rook.
notes.original: White's 2nd most common response. Blunder. This creates a discovery on the h5 knight. Black can't easily capture white's dark-squared bishop without sacrificing both the h5 knight and the capturing h4 pawn. However, this leaves the a1 rook in a compromised position, unable to move. Black can counterattack the b2 pawn with Qb6. If white captures the h5 knight, black can capture the b2 pawn which corners the rook, unable to avoid being captured. White could've avoided this by not moving the f3 knight to d2, as white now can't move the b1 knight without leaving it hanging after Qxb2.

notes.text: White offers a knight trade and uncovers its queen on your h5 knight; trade knights first.
notes.original: White's strongest, 3rd most common response. This offers a knight trade and creates a discovery on the h5 knight. Black can't easily capture white's dark-squared bishop without sacrificing both the h5 knight and the capturing g5 pawn (now undefended on h4). Additionally, black is forced to first trade knights in order to both damage white's pawn structure (as white can recapture with the queen if gxh4 is played first), and prevent a knight sacrifice with Nxf7 (which can save the dark-squared bishop if Qb6 is played first).

notes.text: You remove the knight before it can join White's queen against f7; the bishop still hangs.
You strike the center at once and pressure White's d4 pawn.
notes.original: Immediately striking in the center! Putting pressure on the d4-pawn.

notes.text: White builds a pawn pyramid with c3, d4 and e3 to hold the centre.
notes.original: Forming the pawn pyramid.

notes.text: Knight to f3 here is dubious for anyone who wants a true London setup.
notes.original: As we've seen in previous chapters, this is dubious if you want to play in the style of the London.

notes.text: Your knight joins the c-pawn in pressing on White's d4 pawn.
Recapturing with the a-pawn opens the a-file, so your rook already eyes a2.
Push the b-pawn to b4 and take on c3, leaving White a permanently backward c-pawn.
notes.original: Preparing to advance the b-pawn in order to capture on c3. This will leave White with a backward c-pawn permanently!

notes.text: Your pawn hits c3, ready to trade there and leave White a weak c-pawn.
Developing your bishop to f5 causes London players real problems.
notes.original: Either this or b4 causes problems for London players.

notes.text: Your pawn hits the knight and b2, so White recaptures and keeps a backward c-pawn.
Your rook attacks the backward c3 pawn, which nothing defends right now.
You can still push b4: your rook pins the a3 pawn to the rook behind it.
notes.original: Black can still advance due to the pin on the a-file!

notes.text: Same trick again: your bishop hits the queen and wins an important tempo.
notes.original: Same trick as in the previous subvariation! Black wins an important tempo!

notes.text: With your bishop already outside, the pawn supports d5 and frees your other bishop.
The position is equal.
White has many positional problems here.
Your knight threatens to take the London bishop on f4.
notes.original: Now threatening to swap the London bishop for a knight.

notes.text: Your bishop gets out before the e-pawn shuts it in, and it watches e4.
The pawn backs up d5 and opens the way for your dark bishop.
Your bishop clears the back rank so you can castle kingside next.
You get an easy game, and your c5 pawn gives a more aggressive structure and a c-file to open.
notes.original: Black gets an easy game and has the more aggressive pawn-structure due to his pawn on c5. He can open the c-file whenever he pleases with a good game to follow.

notes.text: Trading on d4 clears your c-pawn away, giving your rook the c-file toward White's queen.
The pawn props up d5 and your bishop, and lets your other bishop out.
Recapturing with the a-pawn opens the a-file for your rook against the a2 pawn.
The position is equal.
Your queen checks the king and will win back the c5 pawn.
notes.original: Black regains the pawn and continue development normally.

notes.text: Your knight comes out to its usual square, guarding d5 and watching e4.
White usually plays this: it defends d4 and frees the light-squared bishop.
notes.original: Usually however White does end up over-defending the d-pawn, because most of the moves they'd like to play next happen to do so anyway. White usually plays 3.e3, which defends d4 but is also essential for opening up White's kings-side bishop. After 3...Nf6, Black has transposed back into the main line against the Accelerated London.

notes.text: White wants e3, c3, Nd2 and Bd3, then a knight to e5 via f3.
notes.original:
Black's most common approach to combating the Accelerated London is with both Nf6 and d5, whether they began with the Indian defence 1...Nf6 or the Closed game 1...d5.

White's plans in the London system are generally to to play e3, c3, Nd2, Bd3 in some order, and plant their kingside knight on e5 via Nf3.

3.e3 is the most common move order. This defends d4 and prepares to develop Bd3.Once Nf3 is played, e.g. 3.Nf3, the opening has converged with the regular, non-accelerated London. 3.Nc3, instead of playing c3, transposes to the Rapport-Jobava London.

Black's two main approaches involve 3...c5 or 3...e6.

The idea behind the 3...e6 line is to play 4...Bd6, getting ready to castle quickly and threatening to trade off White's London bishop. White can drop their bishop back to g2, inviting Black to trade but after hxg2 White gets the semi-open h-file in return. In the e6 lines, Black's light square bishop often has difficulty developing. This approach resembles a Semi-Slav defence with colours reversed.

The ...c5 line has the idea to to prioritise ...Bf5 and ...Qb6 before finishing developing the kingside and castling. Black seeks counterplay by pressuring b2, which White left undefended when they moved their bishop early on. (White does not want to take the offered c5 pawn of course: they'd rather play c3 and let Black trade into them, so that they can keep two pawns in the centre).

Having committed to d5 already, the King's Indian-style approach with 3...g6 is less common but still playable. Black continues 4...Bg7, and 5...O-O. White usually includes h3, so there is a retreat square for their bishop on h2, and Be2.

notes.text: Against this setup you mainly choose between ...e6 followed by ...Bd6, or the ...c5 line.

notes.text: Your pawn takes b5 away from White's knight, so the fork on c7 never comes.
This is your most popular reply: it backs up the d5 pawn and opens your dark-squared bishop.
notes.original:
This is Black's most popular response. This move reinforces the centre and opens up the dark-squared bishop. It does, however, pacify Black's light-squared bishop. The next couple of moves will likely happen on the queenside, since neither side has many attacking opportunities on the kingside.

The thematic 4.Nb5 is White's main response, threatening a fork on the c7-square. Black has two ways to defend against this: 4...Na6 is the most popular response. Black defends c7 with their knight and will soon kick out White's knight with c6 and reposition their a6-knight to c7 and subsequently e8, protecting the kingside. Alternatively, Black can opt for 4...Bb4+, which leads to a forcing line 5.c3 (5.Bd2? Bxd2 6.Qxd2 ) Ba5 and the bishop is now protecting c7. If White continues chasing the bishop with 6.a4 a6 7.b4 Bxb4 8.cxb4 axb5 9.axb5 Rxa1 10.Qxa1 the players have entered an endgame where White has a worse pawn structure, but more advanced pawns on the queenside.

Alternatively, White can play 4.e3, simply continuing development. This gives Black the opportunity of playing 4...Bb4, pinning the knight and possibly doubling White's queenside pawns, similar to the Winawer French. Alternatively, Black can continue 4...Bd6, preparing to trade dark-squared bishops.

notes.text: White wants Nb5 to threaten a knight fork on c7; you can meet it with c5, a6 or e6.
notes.original: Sometimes referred to as the Rapport-Jobava System. This opening serves as a good surprise weapon against unprepared opponents, and in the worst case, equalizes. White often plans to threaten a knight fork on the c7 square after Nb5, usually played on the fourth or fifth move. Black typically challenges the center immediately with 3...c5 and trades their c-pawn for White's e-pawn. Alternatively, Black often plays the 3...a6 Anti-Jobava to control the b5 square or the natural 3...e6 development move. Black may also attempt 3...Bf5, developing the light-squared bishop before playing 4...e6, but it gives White an opportunity to launch a pawn storm with a tempo on the bishop through a well-timed g4 push (usually after White plays f3 or Ne5, protecting the g4 square).

notes.text: The pawn backs up d5 and lets your dark bishop out so you can castle.
Your queen hits b2; that won against the Nf3 move order, but is it still good here?
notes.original: Before with 2. Nf3 this move was winning, how about now?

notes.text: White's knight can come to f3 safely now; this is essentially a London against your d5 and e6 setup.
notes.original: Now Nf3 is safe. However, it can be further delayed if necessary. This is now essentially a d5 e6 London.

notes.text: White is happy with this setup, especially for attacking your kingside.
notes.original: An ideal position for London players, especially those who wish to attack on the kingside.

notes.original: Beginning the attack!

notes.text: Your knight threatens to take the bishop on f4.
notes.original: Threatening to swap on f4...

notes.text: White ignores your threat and sacrifices the bishop on h7, a common London theme.
notes.original: … but white ignores it completely! Sacrificing the bishop on h7 is a common theme in the London.

notes.text: The knight checks you; retreating the king to g8 or h8 loses at once, and taking on g5 is bad.
notes.original: Kg8 and Kh8 both lose immediately, while Bxg5 is just bad.

notes.text: Playing f6 here is a big mistake.
notes.original: A big mistake.

notes.original: White is now clearly winning.

notes.original: This is just winning for white.

notes.text: White offers a queen trade; neither side wants to swap and open the a-file.
notes.original: It's important to know this move as Qb6 will likely come up a lot in your games. Neither side wants to swap queens and open the a-file here.

notes.text: Your pawn hits White's queen, so it must move away or trade at once.
The pawn guards f5, so your bishop can go there next and hit White's queen.
Bf5 is simply a blunder here.
notes.original: Now this move is simply a blunder.

notes.text: White is clearly winning after these trades.
notes.original: White is clearly winning.

notes.original: Remember to play this if your opponent plays Bf5.

The engine likes White here, but this line is still dubious for London players.
notes.original: Computer says we're ahead, but this is still dubious for Londoners.

notes.text: Engines keep changing their verdict on this position, so it is a messy fight.
notes.original: The computer is changing its mind constantly about what the evaluation is.

notes.text: This is why Nf6 comes first: skipping it makes this knight move run into trouble.
notes.original: For those wondering why Nf6 needs to be played at all, here's why.

notes.text: Your queen hits the b2 pawn that White's bishop left unguarded.
You can grab the b2 pawn with your queen or just keep developing.
notes.original: Now we can either accept the sacrificed pawn on b2 or continue to play normally.

notes.text: Your knight develops and adds a second attacker on the d4 pawn.
White's best here is the counterintuitive dxc5 instead of the usual c3.
notes.original: Instead of the typical c3 the counterintuitive dxc5 is best here.

notes.text: Now taking the b2 pawn with your queen looks very attractive.
notes.original: Now taking the b2 pawn looks very attractive.

notes.text: You take the b2 pawn in return for the one White just took on c5.
Your queen steps away from the rook, pins the d2 knight and eyes the c5 pawn.
Both sides have chances, and this line feels very strange to London players.
notes.original: Again, with chances for both sides. This line especially will feel very strange to London players.

Your queen dodges the rook by taking a second pawn and pins the d2 knight.
Both sides have chances in this sharp position.
notes.original: With chances for both sides.
